performers: William McColl, basset clarinet; University of Washington Symphony Orchestra, Abraham Kaplan
intro: The Adagio of the Clarinet Concerto in A major, K. 622, is in D major. The clarinet plays the melody and the orchestra replies with phrases of its own. William McColl plays it on a basset clarinet he built himself, with Abraham Kaplan and the University of Washington Symphony Orchestra.

sections.label: A · Clarinet melody over strings
sections.mNote: Melody in D major for clarinet.

sections.label: A′ · Orchestral reply to the solo clarinet
sections.mNote: Flutes, bassoons and horns join the strings’ reply.

sections.label: B · The clarinet adds ornaments
sections.mNote: Long notes are followed by runs and wide leaps.

sections.label: A″ · D major melody returns
sections.mNote: The soloist resumes after a pause on the dominant.

sections.label: A′ · Orchestral answering phrase, winds added
sections.mNote: Winds join the violins for the answering phrase.

sections.label: Coda · Clarinet solo in D
sections.mNote: The clarinet decorates the closing phrases above soft strings.

relations.label: The orchestra answers the solo melody
relations.basis: The first A section sets the clarinet’s opening phrase against an orchestral answer near 34 s. The melodic material is shared, but its scoring changes. CENS diagonal mean 0.924, sustained 15.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 33 s (cache/form/mozart-clarinet-adagio.txt, candidate 5; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The opening melody returns
relations.basis: After the contrasting middle, the A′ section restores the solo melody. The matched later excerpt falls inside the return marked near 262 s, not at a claimed precise entrance. CENS diagonal mean 0.953, sustained 18.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 266.5 s (cache/form/mozart-clarinet-adagio.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening of the Adagio, solo clarinet
cues.text: The clarinet enters over moving violins and held viola notes, with the cellos playing a light bass. The double basses and orchestral winds rest. The melody rises and falls, and each phrase is separated by rests.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, p. 236: solo clarinet, violins, viola and cello; double basses and winds rest. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f7/IMSLP29515-PMLP03144-Mozart_Clarinet_Concerto_K622.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First tutti in D
cues.text: The orchestra follows the solo phrase in D. Flutes, bassoons and horns join the strings, with the double basses beneath them. The violins take the melody, and in the printed score the clarinet doubles their line.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, first tutti, p. 236. The edition prints the solo clarinet doubling the violin melody during tutti passages.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: McColl’s basset clarinet, December 1987
cues.text: In this December 1987 performance William McColl played an instrument he had built himself. The basset clarinet extends the low range of the ordinary clarinet and gives Mozart’s soloist more notes below the stave.
cues.evidence: The Soni Ventorum archive identifies McColl’s self-built basset clarinet and the December 1987 performance: https://soniventorum.com/soniventorum_archives.html. The extended low range is described by Calvin Dotsey: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.

cues.title: Middle section, A major
cues.text: The middle section begins in A major. The clarinet decorates its line with quick runs and wider leaps, and the strings accompany softly. Long notes alternate with short runs.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, pp. 237–238. Calvin Dotsey describes the more ornamental central section: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Constanze, October 1791
cues.text: On 7 October 1791, while finishing the concerto, Mozart wrote to Constanze in Baden after another full house for The Magic Flute. He wrote that what pleased him most was its “silent applause”, the audience’s absorbed attention during the music.
cues.evidence: Mozart to Constanze, Vienna, 7–8 October 1791, Bauer–Deutsch 1193: “was mich aber am meisten freuet, ist, der Stille beifall!” He also reports orchestrating the concerto’s rondo. Our translation: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/raradocs/transcr/pdf/BD_1193.pdf.

cues.title: Return of the first melody
cues.text: A pause on the dominant prepares the return of the D major melody. The clarinet resumes over the softly moving strings, and the double basses rest again. Mozart shortens the return, and the soloist then plays a more ornate closing passage.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, pp. 239–241: dominant fermata, return and coda. The shortened reprise is described by Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, final clarinet phrase
cues.text: The clarinet plays ornamental figures and a trill above quiet strings. The melody stays close to D major. Winds and horns return for the closing cadence and accompany the soloist’s last notes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, coda, p. 241.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The violins take over the melody
transitions.to: A′ · Orchestral reply to the solo clarinet
transitions.how: The solo phrase closes on A, the dominant of D major. Moving notes in the strings lead into the orchestral tutti in D. Flutes, bassoons, horns and double basses join, and the violins take over the melody above the continuing accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, first solo and tutti, p. 236.

transitions.title: The A major middle section
transitions.from: A′ · Orchestral reply to the solo clarinet
transitions.how: The orchestral passage closes and the winds stop. Above soft strings, the clarinet begins the A major middle section and extends its phrases into runs and leaps. Beneath these quicker notes the accompaniment keeps to the slow three-beat measure.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, pp. 237–238.

transitions.title: Fermata on A, return in D
transitions.how: Orchestral chords alternate with clarinet runs and lead to a fermata on A major, the dominant. After the pause the opening tune returns in D over a flowing accompaniment in the violins. The winds and double basses rest, and the scoring is again as light as at the beginning.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, p. 239.

transitions.title: Winds rest before the closing solo
transitions.from: A′ · Orchestral answering phrase, winds added
transitions.how: The orchestral reply reaches D major, and the winds stop. A rising clarinet figure begins the coda over quiet strings. The soloist ornaments the closing phrases, and winds and horns return for the final cadence in D major.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), II, pp. 240–241.

source.title: Mozart, Clarinet Concerto in A, K. 622, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke Serie XII No. 20, 1881, plate W.A.M. 622)
source.locator: II. Adagio, printed pp. 236–241: solo phrases, orchestral answers and coda. The double basses rest beneath the opening solo and its return.

Flutes, bassoons, horns and double basses join the violins’ answer.
The clarinet enters again above the strings; the double basses stop again.
The orchestra replies forte, with flutes, bassoons and horns above the strings.
The clarinet returns over soft strings as the orchestral winds rest.
The soloist ornaments the new melody above quiet strings.
Horns hold soft notes beneath the clarinet’s running figures.
Wind chords alternate with clarinet runs, leading to a fermata.
The opening melody returns over strings; double basses and winds rest.
Flutes, bassoons and horns join the violins’ fuller reply.
The clarinet decorates the coda above soft strings; double basses rejoin near the close.
Flutes, bassoons and horns return for the soft D major cadence.

quote.source: Mozart to his father Leopold, Vienna, 13 October 1781; our translation

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to play the finale through. The work was K. 466 in D minor. It opens with syncopated strings, and the piano enters with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert excellent.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart later dedicated the quartets to him.
